Notification System
topics.concepts: Kafka, queues, fan-out, retries, DLQ, multi-channel delivery
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a notification system that sends push notifications, SMS and emails for an e-commerce app: "Your order has shipped", "Your OTP is 482193", "Flash sale starts in 1 hour".

Many internal services trigger notifications. The system must deliver them through external providers (Apple, Google, SMS gateways, email services) reliably, respect user preferences, and not spam anyone.

## Requirements

**Functional**

- Send push (iOS and Android), SMS and email.
- Other services trigger notifications through one API, using templates ("order_shipped" + order details).
- Respect user preferences (opted out of marketing email, quiet hours).
- Support scheduled notifications and priority (an OTP must not wait behind a marketing blast).
- Track status: sent, failed, delivered (when the provider tells us).

**Non-functional**

- Scale: about 10 million push, 5 million email and 1 million SMS per day; marketing campaigns cause large bursts.
- Reliable: an accepted notification is not lost; retries must not spam users.
- Soft real-time: OTPs within seconds; marketing can take minutes.

Out of scope: building the providers themselves, in-app inbox UI, campaign management tools.

## 1. Clarify requirements and estimate the scale

| Question to ask | Answer we choose | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which channels? | Push, SMS, email. | One queue and worker type per channel. |
| Exactly-once delivery? | No. At-least-once to providers, with de-duplication to avoid obvious duplicates. | Providers and networks can time out after accepting. |
| Who decides the message text? | Templates owned by the notification system. | Callers send data, not raw text. |
| Can users opt out? | Yes, per channel and per category. | Check preferences before sending. |
| Priorities? | High (OTP, security), normal (order updates), low (marketing). | Separate queues so marketing never delays an OTP. |

| Quantity | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average sends | 16M / 86,400 s | ≈ 185/s |
| Campaign burst | 5M emails in 30 min | ≈ 2,800/s for email |
| Log storage | 16M × 500 B per day | ≈ 8 GB/day; keep 90 days ≈ 720 GB |

A 45-minute plan:

| Minutes | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| 0–8 | Requirements and estimates |
| 8–15 | API and data model |
| 15–25 | High-level design with queues |
| 25–38 | Reliability: retries, de-duplication, rate limits, priorities |
| 38–45 | Scaling, monitoring, follow-ups |

## 2. API and data model

Internal services call one endpoint:

```http
POST /v1/notifications
{
  "eventId": "order-847-shipped",
  "userId": 42,
  "template": "order_shipped",
  "channels": ["push", "email"],
  "priority": "NORMAL",
  "data": { "orderId": "847", "eta": "Friday" },
  "sendAt": null
}

202 Accepted
{ "notificationId": "N501" }
```

`202 Accepted` means "we have it and will deliver", not "delivered". `eventId` lets us ignore the same event if the caller sends it twice.

| Table | Key fields |
| --- | --- |
| `user_contact` | userId, email, phone |
| `device` | userId, deviceToken, platform (iOS/Android), lastSeen |
| `preference` | userId, channel, category, enabled, quietHours |
| `template` | name, channel, version, subject/body with placeholders |
| `notification` | id, eventId (unique), userId, template, data, createdAt |
| `delivery` | notificationId, channel, status (QUEUED/SENT/FAILED/DELIVERED), attempts, providerMessageId |

## 3. High-level design

[![Selected design: business services call the notification service, which reads preferences and devices, records the notification and enqueues one message per channel; channel workers consume, deliver through APNs, FCM, SMS and email providers, and record status and retries.](designs/hld-4.svg)](designs/hld-4.svg)

Walk through "order 847 shipped" for user 42:

1. The order service calls `POST /v1/notifications`.
2. The notification service checks `eventId` (already seen → return the existing id), loads user 42's preferences and devices, and drops channels the user opted out of.
3. It saves the notification and one `delivery` row per channel, then puts one message per channel on the right **queue** (Kafka topics or SQS queues): `push.normal`, `email.normal`.
4. **Workers** for each channel read from their queue, render the template, and call the provider: APNs for iPhones, FCM for Android, an SMS gateway such as Twilio, an email service such as SES or SendGrid.
5. Workers record SENT or FAILED. Providers later report delivery and opens through webhooks.

![Animation: the order service sends one event; the notification service checks preferences and enqueues a push message and an email message; separate workers deliver each through its provider; a provider timeout puts the email back for a retry with backoff.](learning-figures/hld-4-fanout.gif)

**Why queues in the middle?**

- **Decoupling**: the order service returns in milliseconds and never waits for Apple or an SMS gateway.
- **Absorbing bursts**: a 5-million-email campaign waits in the queue instead of overwhelming workers or the provider.
- **Isolation**: one queue per channel (and priority) means an SMS outage does not block push notifications, and marketing cannot delay OTPs.
- **Retries**: a failed message can be retried later without involving the caller.

[![Notification pipeline: an event is accepted once, preferences decide the channels, one message per channel goes to its own queue, workers render templates and call providers, and failures go back with backoff or to a dead-letter queue.](learning-figures/hld-4-pipeline.svg)](learning-figures/hld-4-pipeline.svg)

## 4. Deep dive: reliability without spamming

**Don't lose notifications.** Save the notification and delivery rows **before** acknowledging the caller, and only remove a message from the queue after the worker has recorded the result. If a worker crashes mid-send, the message becomes visible again and another worker picks it up.

**Retries with backoff.** Providers fail temporarily (timeouts, 5xx, rate limits). Retry with exponential backoff and jitter – for example 1 s, 4 s, 16 s, … – up to a limit. Permanent errors (invalid device token, bad email address) are not retried: mark FAILED and, for a dead token, delete it from `device`. After the last attempt, send the message to a **dead-letter queue** for inspection.

**At-least-once means possible duplicates.** If the provider accepted a push but our worker timed out before recording it, a retry sends it again. Reduce this by:

- de-duplicating callers with the unique `eventId`;
- passing a stable idempotency key to providers that support one (many email and SMS APIs do);
- checking the `delivery` row status before sending (skip if already SENT).

A rare duplicate "your order shipped" is acceptable; a lost OTP is worse. Say this trade-off out loud.

**Rate limiting per user.** No user should get 30 marketing pushes a day. Keep a counter per user per category (token bucket in Redis) and drop or delay notifications over the cap. OTP and security messages bypass marketing limits.

**Preferences and quiet hours.** Check them when the notification is accepted *and* again in the worker just before sending – the user may have opted out in between. During quiet hours, low-priority messages are rescheduled instead of sent.

## 5. Scaling and operations

| Concern | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Throughput | Notification service and workers are stateless; add instances. Partition queues by userId. |
| Provider limits | Each provider allows N requests/s; workers use a shared rate limiter per provider so they do not get blocked. |
| Priorities | Separate high/normal/low queues; give high-priority workers dedicated capacity. |
| Scheduled sends | Store `sendAt`; a scheduler polls due notifications every few seconds and enqueues them. |
| Big campaigns | A campaign job reads the audience in pages and enqueues in batches, so it does not flood the queue at once. |
| Templates | Versioned; a message records the template version it used, so audits show exactly what was sent. |
| Monitoring | Queue depth and age, send rate, failure rate per provider, delivery and open rates, dead-letter count. |

**Provider outage.** If SMS gateway A fails, workers can switch to a backup gateway B (keep two for critical channels like OTP).

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**How do you get device tokens?** The mobile app registers with APNs or FCM on install, receives a token, and sends it to our backend, which stores it in `device`. Tokens change and expire; refresh them on app start and delete tokens the provider rejects.

**Why not call providers directly from the order service?** It would slow the order flow, duplicate retry logic in every service, and let a provider outage break checkout.

**Kafka or SQS/RabbitMQ?** Either works. Kafka is great for very high throughput and replay; SQS or RabbitMQ give per-message acknowledgements and delays that make retries simple. Say what you would use and why.

**How do you guarantee order (e.g. "shipped" before "delivered")?** Partition the queue by userId so one user's messages are processed in order by one consumer. Strict order across channels is not guaranteed and usually not needed.

**How do you track opens and clicks?** Email: a tracking pixel and redirect links. Push: the app reports opens. Store events in an analytics pipeline, not in the main delivery table.

**What about users with many devices?** Send a push to each active device token. Remove tokens not seen for months.

## 7. Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version of this lesson treats the hardest reliability cases precisely: the **transactional outbox** (the order database writes the event and an outbox row in one transaction, so "order shipped" can never be committed without its notification), worker **leases with epochs** so a slow old worker cannot overwrite a newer attempt, and what to do when a provider timed out **after** accepting a message (query by the same key rather than blindly resending).

[![Two durable handoffs: the order database commits the order change and its outbox together; a relay delivers the event to notification ingest, which de-duplicates it and creates deliveries and a delivery outbox in one transaction.](learning-figures/hld-4-handoff.svg)](learning-figures/hld-4-handoff.svg)

[![Timeout after acceptance: a provider accepts message P1 but the response is lost; the delivery is marked unknown and the next worker queries the same key instead of sending a second message.](learning-figures/hld-4-uncertainty.svg)](learning-figures/hld-4-uncertainty.svg)

[Open the notification walkthrough](learning-labs/notification.html), or read the runnable Java: [DispatchEngine.java](reference-code/learning/kb/notification/DispatchEngine.java), [FakeProvider.java](reference-code/learning/kb/notification/FakeProvider.java), [NotificationChecks.java](reference-code/learning/kb/notification/NotificationChecks.java) and [NotificationTrace.java](reference-code/learning/kb/notification/NotificationTrace.java).

## 8. Closing answer

"Services call one notification API with an event ID, a template and data; it returns 202 after saving the notification. The service checks preferences and devices, then puts one message per channel and priority onto its own queue. Stateless workers render templates and call APNs, FCM, SMS and email providers, recording each result. Queues decouple callers, absorb campaign bursts and isolate channels so marketing never delays an OTP. Delivery is at-least-once: messages are acknowledged only after the result is recorded, failures retry with exponential backoff and jitter, permanent errors stop, and dead letters are kept. Event IDs, provider idempotency keys and status checks keep duplicates rare, and per-user rate limits and quiet hours prevent spam."

topics.title: Embeddings & Semantic Search
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Your company's help centre has 5,000 support articles. Users type questions like *"I forgot my login"* but the right article is titled *"Resetting your password"*. Keyword search fails because the words do not match.

Design semantic search: find articles by **meaning**, not exact words. Explain embeddings, similarity, chunking and vector stores, and implement it with Spring AI.

## Requirements

- Explain what an embedding is and how similarity is measured.
- Index documents: chunking, embedding and storing with metadata.
- Search: embed the query, find the top-K most similar chunks, apply filters.
- Explain when keyword search still matters and how hybrid search combines both.
- Explain vector indexes (exact vs approximate) and evaluation.
- Implement with Spring AI's `EmbeddingModel` and `VectorStore`.

## 1. The idea in plain words

An **embedding** is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. An embedding model is trained so that texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions.

```text
"I forgot my login"           -> [0.12, -0.03, 0.88, ...]   (e.g. 1,536 numbers)
"Resetting your password"     -> [0.10, -0.01, 0.85, ...]   close
"Shipping times to Europe"    -> [-0.40, 0.72, 0.05, ...]   far away
```

Think of it as GPS coordinates for meaning: we cannot read individual numbers, but we can measure distance between points.

**Semantic search** = embed every document once, embed the query, and return the documents whose vectors are closest to the query vector.

**What interviewers usually ask:** what an embedding is; cosine similarity; why chunk documents; what a vector database does; exact vs approximate search (HNSW); semantic vs keyword search; how this fits into RAG.

## 2. Measuring similarity

The usual measure is **cosine similarity**: the cosine of the angle between two vectors. 1 means same direction (very similar), 0 means unrelated, −1 means opposite.

Small 2-D example (real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions):

```text
query  "forgot login"       q = (1, 0)
doc A  "reset password"     a = (1, 0)     cosine = 1.00   -> best match
doc B  "login error codes"  b = (1, 1)     cosine = 1/√2 ≈ 0.71
doc C  "billing"            c = (0, 1)     cosine = 0.00

cosine(x, y) = (x · y) / (|x| × |y|)
```

```java
static double cosine(float[] x, float[] y) {
    if (x.length != y.length) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Different embedding sizes");
    double dot = 0, nx = 0, ny = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) {
        dot += x[i] * y[i];
        nx  += x[i] * x[i];
        ny  += y[i] * y[i];
    }
    return dot / (Math.sqrt(nx) * Math.sqrt(ny));
}
```

If vectors are **normalised** to length 1 (many models return them that way), cosine equals the plain dot product – cheaper to compute.

[![Unit vectors: the query and reset vectors point along (1,0); the error vector (1,1) normalised is about (0.707, 0.707), 45 degrees away, so its cosine with the query is 1 divided by the square root of two.](learning-figures/ai-4-vector-geometry.svg)](learning-figures/ai-4-vector-geometry.svg)

**Rule: query and documents must use the same embedding model.** Vectors from different models live in different "spaces" and cannot be compared, even if they have the same length. Changing models means re-embedding everything.

## 3. The indexing and search pipeline (the retrieval algorithm)

[![Selected design: documents are split into chunks and embedded; vectors with metadata go into a vector store; at query time the user's question is embedded with the same model and a similarity search returns the top-K nearest chunks.](designs/ai-4.svg)](designs/ai-4.svg)

**Indexing (offline, when documents change)**

1. **Load** articles.
2. **Chunk** them into pieces of a few hundred tokens, with a small overlap. One vector for a 20-page document blurs many topics together; chunks keep each vector focused and fit the model's input limit.
3. **Embed** each chunk.
4. **Store** the vector with the chunk text and **metadata** (article ID, title, product, language, permissions, last updated).

**Search (online, per query)**

1. Embed the query with the same model.
2. Ask the vector store for the **top-K** nearest chunks (say K = 5), optionally above a **similarity threshold** and filtered by metadata (`product == 'payments'`, user may see it).
3. Return the chunks with their article links.

![Animation: articles are chunked and embedded into a vector store; the query "I forgot my login" is embedded with the same model; the store returns the nearest chunks, with "Resetting your password" first, even though no keyword matches.](learning-figures/ai-4-search.gif)

**Vector stores**: pgvector (PostgreSQL extension), Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Redis, or dedicated databases like Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus. If you already run PostgreSQL, pgvector is often the simplest start.

## 4. In code with Spring AI

```java
@Service
public class HelpSearch {
    private final VectorStore vectorStore;      // e.g. PgVectorStore or SimpleVectorStore, auto-configured
    private final TokenTextSplitter splitter = new TokenTextSplitter();

    public HelpSearch(VectorStore vectorStore) {
        this.vectorStore = vectorStore;
    }

    public void index(Article article) {
        Document doc = new Document(article.body(), Map.of(
                "articleId", article.id(),
                "title", article.title(),
                "product", article.product()));
        List<Document> chunks = splitter.apply(List.of(doc));   // chunks keep the metadata
        vectorStore.add(chunks);                                 // embeds with the configured EmbeddingModel
    }

    public List<Document> search(String question, String product) {
        return vectorStore.similaritySearch(SearchRequest.builder()
                .query(question)
                .topK(5)
                .similarityThreshold(0.6)
                .filterExpression("product == '" + product + "'")   // use a validated product value
                .build());
    }
}
```

`vectorStore.add` calls the configured `EmbeddingModel` for you. You can also call it directly:

```java
float[] vector = embeddingModel.embed("I forgot my login");   // e.g. 1,536 numbers
```

For a quick start, `SimpleVectorStore.builder(embeddingModel).build()` keeps vectors in memory; for production use a persistent store such as pgvector (`spring-ai-starter-vector-store-pgvector`). For filters built from user input, prefer Spring AI's `FilterExpressionBuilder` over string concatenation.

## 5. Keyword vs semantic search, scale and evaluation

**Semantic search is not always better.** For exact identifiers – error code `E1042`, an order ID, a function name – keyword search (BM25, as in Elasticsearch) is more reliable, because embeddings capture meaning, not exact strings.

**Hybrid search** runs both and combines the rankings. A simple, popular method is **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**: each result scores `1 / (60 + rank)` in each list, and the scores are added. A document ranked well in both lists rises to the top.

```text
Query "E1042 login error"
  keyword list:   error-1 (rank 1)
  semantic list:  billing-1 (rank 1), error-1 (rank 2)
  RRF: error-1  = 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0325   <- best
       billing-1 = 1/61       ≈ 0.0164
```

**Exact vs approximate search.** Comparing the query with every vector (exact, "brute force") is fine for thousands of chunks. For millions, vector stores use **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes such as **HNSW**: much faster, at the cost of occasionally missing a true neighbour. Tune the index for the recall you need.

**Permissions.** Apply access filters **inside** the search (metadata filter), not after taking the top 5 – otherwise a user may get fewer results, or see a title they should not.

**Evaluate.** Build a small set of real questions with the correct article for each. Measure **recall@5** (is the right article in the top 5?) and **MRR** (how high it ranks). Re-run when you change chunk size, model or K.

[![Rank only the current eligible corpus: tenant, role and current-revision checks run before scoring, so staff-only, other-tenant or stale chunks never appear in the returned text or IDs.](learning-figures/ai-4-permission-filter.svg)](learning-figures/ai-4-permission-filter.svg)

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Cosine similarity vs Euclidean distance?** For normalised vectors they rank results the same way. Cosine ignores vector length and is the usual default for text.

**How big should chunks be?** Commonly 200–800 tokens with 10–20% overlap. Too small loses context; too large blurs topics. Measure with your evaluation set.

**What does a similarity score of 0.82 mean?** Only "closer than lower scores" for this model. Scores are not probabilities, and good thresholds differ between models – calibrate them on your data.

**How do embeddings relate to RAG?** RAG uses this search to find relevant chunks, then puts them in the LLM's prompt so it answers from your documents.

**What happens when a document is updated?** Re-chunk and re-embed it, delete the old chunks (by article ID in metadata), and insert the new ones.

**How much storage do vectors need?** 1,536 floats × 4 bytes ≈ 6 KB per chunk. 1 million chunks ≈ 6 GB, plus the index.

## 7. Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version builds a complete local search engine without any model account: toy vectors you can verify by hand, numerically careful normalisation, permission filtering before scoring, revision checks so stale chunks never return, and a hybrid fusion of exact-word and vector rankings.

[Open the semantic-search lab](learning-labs/semantic-search.html), or read the runnable Java: [SemanticSearch.java](reference-code/learning/kb/semanticsearch/SemanticSearch.java). Spring AI's vector-store API is described in the [Spring AI vector databases reference](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/api/vectordbs.html).

## 8. Closing answer

"An embedding is a vector that represents the meaning of text; similar meanings point in similar directions, measured with cosine similarity. To build semantic search I chunk documents into a few hundred tokens with overlap, embed each chunk, and store vectors with text and metadata in a vector store such as pgvector. At query time I embed the question with the same model and ask for the top-K nearest chunks, with a threshold and metadata filters for product and permissions. Because embeddings miss exact identifiers, I combine them with keyword search using reciprocal rank fusion. For large collections I rely on approximate indexes like HNSW, and I evaluate with recall@K on real questions. In Spring AI that is `EmbeddingModel`, `TokenTextSplitter` and `VectorStore.similaritySearch`."
